A recognised member forum with authority over one class of decisions (say, appeals of first-offence actions) is the smallest possible collective-choice arrangement. Neither requires redesigning the community; each lowers the cost of the next change.

Build the sanctions ladder as in m3's worked example, applied by rotating members rather than staff alone: first violation, a public templated note within a day; second, a fixed short restriction; third, a review by three members; bans never a first response. Cheap to apply, therefore credible; escalation scheduled and delegated.

Now you design the nesting (principle 8). Sub-communities handle local disputes and first-line moderation with their own logs; a higher layer handles cross-community conflict, shared infrastructure and appeals against sub-community decisions; platform staff sit at the top as backstop and data supplier, not as rule-writer. Say who has standing at each layer and where a member goes when two layers disagree.

Tags. [E] for the principles as a diagnostic (91-study review, with publication-bias and structure-not-process caveats). [H] for transfer to a digital commons and for the prediction that the log and forum outperform staff-only moderation here. [V] for member governance over staff efficiency; the checklist cannot tell you that the slower, member-run arrangement is worth it.

hinge.q: A funder says: "Ostrom showed communities manage shared resources better than states or markets, so we should just hand the resource to the community." What is wrong?
options: Nothing; that is the book's thesis.
Communities fail because the PD is a law; only privatisation works.
It works if the community adopts all eight principles.
Self-governance is a third option that works under identifiable conditions; durable cases lean on courts and enabling law as backstops, and Ostrom warned against panaceas.
diagnoses: Ostrom as anti-state and pro-panacea (ledger C47). Her durable cases use courts, enabling legislation and recognised property rights; she said neither central control nor privatisation is the *only* solution, not that community management always wins.

The PD as a law of nature (ledger C49). She refuted the PD as a law; it stays valid for open access, and participants move themselves into a different game when they can communicate, monitor and change rules.

Principles as a recipe to install (ledger rule 29). They specify no rules; they are structural conditions found in durable cases, supported by a review with caveats, and the processes (trust, legitimacy) that make structure work are not on the list.

Correct. Self-organisation succeeds and fails for identifiable reasons (`09` ch 4, ch 5, evidence section); the supply of institutions is sensitive to size, heterogeneity and information; and external arenas are what lowered transformation costs in the California basins.

hinge.q: A team's first response to a missed on-call handover is a formal HR warning. Six months later nobody reports handover problems. What happened?
options: The warning worked; problems stopped.
A nuclear first sanction drove violations and reports underground and eroded the information flow that monitoring depends on.
The team lacks a norm psychology and needs stronger penalties.
The warning was not credible; make it a firing.
diagnoses: Silence as compliance; rules-in-form confused with rules-in-use. The absence of reports is exactly what a severe first sanction produces, because reporting a colleague now means triggering HR.

Correct. First sanctions in durable systems are small because their job is to signal that the violator was seen and the rule is alive; a severe first response makes monitors stop reporting and destroys the shared belief compliance depends on (`09` ch 3, principle 5; ledger rule 30).
"Deterrence needs big penalties." The field pattern is the reverse: small first sanctions, escalation held for repeat offenders, and cheap sanctioning (gossip, withdrawal) doing most of the work.

Partly right, wrong level. Credibility matters (`04` ch 8), but it is achieved by making the sanction cheap enough to be applied every time, not by making it bigger; a firing threat is less credible still.

hinge.q: A reform (a new rota rule) stalls for a year although everyone agrees it is better. Where does Ostrom say to look first?
options: At the collective-choice level: do the people bound by the rota have a legitimate, low-cost way to change it, and does anyone outside recognise their right to?
At the operational rule; rewrite it more clearly.
At the individuals blocking it.
At the discount rate: people do not care about the future.
diagnoses: Correct. Most fixes are operational and most failures are a level up: nobody affected can legitimately change the rule, or the group has no recognised standing (`09` ch 2, ch 6). "Everyone agrees" tells you the block is standing, not wording.
Most fixes are operational; most failures are a level up. A clearer rule that nobody has standing to adopt stalls exactly as the unclear one did.
Dispositional diagnosis (m2). The situational alternative here is structural: the reform has no legitimate route to adoption, so anyone in the way looks like a blocker.

Partly right, wrong level. Discount rates affect willingness to invest in rule change, but "everyone agrees it is better" says the benefit is already perceived; what is missing is the arena in which agreement becomes a rule.

hinge.q: Which claim about Ostrom's principles may be tagged [E]?
options: They cause durability.
They transfer directly to open-source projects and knowledge commons.
Durable commons are egalitarian.
Where a study assessed a principle, its presence was mostly associated with success and its absence with failure, across 91 studies, with publication-bias and coding caveats.
diagnoses: Causal reading of cases selected on the dependent variable. The book argues the causal claim; the review supports association, with caveats; neither licenses "cause".

Scope over-extension (ledger C48). The book concerns subtractable resources with costly exclusion; knowledge commons found partial fit with principles 1 and 2 reinterpreted, so transfer is [H] with a scope flag.
Durability as fairness (`09` misreadings). Several durable systems have hereditary shares, unequal holdings and exclusion of outsiders; durability and fairness are different criteria.

Correct. Cox, Arnold and Villamayor-Tomás 2010 (verified): well supported, with publication bias, loose qualitative coding, and structure-not-process as the stated limits. That is the [E] wording (ledger rule 29).

modules.brief_prompt: Add section s9, institutional design. Run the eight-principle checklist (Cox's split version) against the group, marking each present, absent or not applicable with a scope note where the shared thing is not a subtractable resource. Then record: the sanctions ladder (first response, escalation, who applies it, the route back to good standing); the by-product monitoring channel; the dispute forum; which rule level the v0 fix lives at and who has standing to change it; and the recognised external backstop. Tag each: [E] for the checklist as diagnostic, [H] for any prediction that supplying a missing principle will help, [V] for governance choices. Prediction: the first cheap change that will produce information and standing, and what it will reveal in three months.

modules.title: Networks: ties, homophily, cascades, small worlds
modules.hook: A documentation norm is adopted enthusiastically by one sub-team and by the one person who liaises with the other four sub-teams. A year later it lives in one sub-team. The liaison was diligent. Why did it not cross?

attempt.prompt: Five sub-teams of eight rarely interact; each has one liaison to the others. A new review norm pays 3 to each pair that both use it and 2 to each pair that both keep the old way (illustrative payoffs; a mismatched pair gets nothing). Where do you seed it, how many seeds, and through whom? Show any arithmetic you use. Ten lines, no reading first.

objectives: Distinguish the three kinds of copying (informational cascade, network effect, coordination on a graph) and name the fix for each.
Compute the cascade threshold q = b/(a+b) from payoffs and apply the cluster-density theorem in both directions to decide where to seed a norm and why a single liaison will not carry it.
Tell closure from bridging, quote the robust form of the weak-ties claim, run the 2pq homophily test, and assume selection over influence until longitudinal data say otherwise.
Say what makes a group navigable and why short paths are never the bottleneck.

ideas.title: The threshold and the cluster-density theorem: where a norm catches and where it stalls
ideas.body:
Chapter 19 of Easley and Kleinberg is the most actionable chapter in the book for norm design, because it gives an exact stall condition. Here each person sees and cares only about **neighbours**, and copies for payoff (a coordination game on each edge), not for information. This is the model of norm spread on a real graph, and it is m4's threshold idea with the population replaced by a network.

**The model, plainly.** On each edge the two endpoints play a coordination game: both use A, each gets a; both use B, each gets b; mismatch, 0. A node with d neighbours, a fraction p of them on A, gets p·d·a from choosing A and (1 − p)·d·b from choosing B. So it prefers A when **p ≥ q = b / (a + b)**. Start with a seed set on A in a network of B-users; every other node switches to A when at least a fraction q of its neighbours use A (switches are one-way). If eventually everyone uses A, the seed set causes a **complete cascade** at threshold q. Note what q is: the fraction of a node's *neighbours*, not of the population. The Origins books' conformist transmission and Schelling's population thresholds are cousins; say which you mean (ledger glossary, "threshold").

**Cluster, defined.** A set of nodes is a *cluster of density p* if every node in it has at least a fraction p of its neighbours inside the set. Sub-teams that mostly talk to each other are clusters of high density.

**The theorem, both directions.** (i) If the network *outside the seed set* contains a cluster of density greater than 1 − q, the seed set does *not* cause a complete cascade. (ii) Conversely, if the seed set does not cause a complete cascade, the network outside it contains a cluster of density greater than 1 − q. Why (i): the first cluster member to switch would have all its A-neighbours outside the cluster, which is fewer than a fraction q of its neighbours, since more than 1 − q are inside; so it cannot switch, and nobody does. Why (ii): at the end of the process the nodes still on B each have fewer than q of their neighbours on A, so together they form a cluster of density greater than 1 − q. The obstacle to a cascade is not distance but the density of tightly-knit communities.

**Arithmetic on the book's example (illustrative).** With a = 3 and b = 2, q = 0.4 and 1 − q = 0.6. Two seeds both link to node c; c links to d; d, e and f form a triangle. Round one: two of c's three neighbours are on A, and 2/3 ≥ 0.4, so c switches. Round two: one of d's three neighbours is on A, and 1/3 < 0.4, so d stays. The cascade stops. Check: the triangle is a cluster of density 2/3, and 2/3 > 0.6 as the theorem predicts. Now change the payoffs to a = 3, b = 1: q = 0.25, 1 − q = 0.75, and 2/3 no longer exceeds 0.75. Now d switches (1/3 ≥ 0.25), then e, then f: a complete cascade. The cold attempt uses the same numbers: with review paying 3 and the old way 2, a node needs two fifths of its neighbours converted, and a sub-team of eight in which each member has seven internal ties and at most one external tie is a cluster of density seven eighths, far above three fifths. Seeds placed outside it never get in; one seed inside it converts nobody because seven neighbours are still on B; three seeds inside get each remaining member to 3/7 ≥ 0.4 and the sub-team tips.

Hence the four design moves. (a) **Lower the threshold** by making A cheaper or B costlier (tooling, templates, compatibility, or "bilinguality", adopting both at a cost), so impenetrable clusters become porous. (b) **Seed inside dense clusters**: a cluster blocks only while none of its members has switched. (c) **Do not expect a norm to jump a single weak tie**; build wide bridges (several parallel ties between sub-groups) or move whole sub-teams. (d) For risky collective action, create common knowledge through visible simultaneous signals (Chwe), because people join only if they know enough others will, and know that those others know.

The rule the ledger attaches (3, and the `10` misreading list): never read the theorem as "clusters are bad". The density that stops a good norm entering also protects an established one from a bad one. And every time you invoke clustering, state the learning-rule condition from m6: threshold dynamics are a form of best response, and Skyrms's point that success-copying and majority-copying diverge still applies at the boundary. The theorem is [E]; Centola's online experiment finding that clustered networks spread costly behaviour faster than random ones is background; your group's q and cluster densities are [H].

ideas.title: Simple versus complex contagion, and the robust form of the weak-ties claim
ideas.body:
Two claims about weak ties are constantly run together, and only one survives. Start with the structure.

**Triadic closure**: if A is strongly tied to B and to C, B and C are likely to become tied, through opportunity, trust and the strain of an open triangle. **Strong Triadic Closure** makes it a rule: if a node has strong ties to two others, at least a weak tie must exist between them. From this alone follows the structural claim: every **local bridge** (an edge whose endpoints share no neighbours, so that neighbourhood overlap is zero) is a weak tie, because a strong bridge from A to B plus any other strong tie of A would force a closing edge, and the bridge would stop being local. Strong ties get closed into triangles; weak ties are disproportionately the bridges between clusters. Onnela and colleagues confirmed this on a national mobile-phone graph: ties with high neighbourhood overlap carried the most call time, and deleting weak ties first shattered the network while deleting strong ties first merely thinned it. **Weak ties tend to be the bridges: robust** (ledger rule 33, C51).

Granovetter's original paper also reported that most jobs in his interviews came through acquaintances rather than close friends, and "useful information comes from weak ties" became folklore. That finding is small-sample and retrospective; later large-scale work found most jobs still came via strong ties (Gee, Jones and Burke, Facebook) or moderately weak ties (Rajkumar et al., LinkedIn). **Quote the structural claim only.** Novelty enters through bridges because your close friends know what you know; that is the sound part.

Now the second distinction, which is ledger rule 34 and diagnostic item d7. **Simple contagion** (information, awareness, a rumour, a disease) needs one exposure, so one bridge into a cluster is enough and clusters merely slow it. **Complex contagion** (costly behaviour, a norm that pays only if neighbours match) needs several adopting neighbours, because the node switches only when a fraction q of its neighbours has. A bridge is one of many edges for the node it reaches, so it rarely makes that node *switch*. Weak ties carry awareness across clusters; they do not carry behaviour. Centola and Macy's work on complex contagions needing wide bridges is the theoretical statement; Centola's online experiment (background) found clustered networks spread costly behaviour faster than random ones, the reverse of information. The hook's diligent liaison failed for exactly this reason: for every node on the far side, the liaison was one neighbour among seven still on the old practice.

Three practical rules follow. First, **find the group's local bridges and protect the people who hold them**: they are usually weak ties, hence fragile, decay unattended, and losing one can cut off a sub-group from all novelty. Second, when the goal is *information flow* (who knows what is happening elsewhere), a few weak bridges suffice and the intervention is to keep them alive. Third, when the goal is *norm adoption*, single liaisons are the wrong instrument; the choices are wide bridges (several parallel ties between the sub-groups), moving whole sub-teams, or seeding inside each cluster. The worked example asks you to decide which face of connectedness is actually the problem before choosing.

A note on the "six degrees" folklore that usually arrives with this material (ledger C50). Milgram's "six" is a median over the minority of chains that completed; most chains in the email replication died; full-graph measurements give roughly four to seven. Say "short paths exist in any large network"; never quote the number as a fact. The fifth idea explains why short paths are the wrong thing to worry about anyway.

ideas.title: Closure gives trust and enforcement; bridges give information; cooperation needs both
ideas.body:
Coleman and Burt describe two kinds of social capital that trade off against each other. A **closed cluster**, in which everyone's friends are friends with each other, gives trust, enforceability and shared norms: violations are seen by people who talk to each other, reputations are common knowledge, and sanctions (m8) are cheap because they are by-products of ordinary interaction. **Spanning a structural hole** between clusters gives information and brokerage power: the person on the only route between two groups sees what neither sees and controls what passes (the market chapters make the same point about intermediaries who are the only path between buyer and seller). All-closure groups enforce stale norms; all-bridge groups enforce nothing.

This is the network face of a tension the whole course keeps meeting (ledger X15, tension t09). The Origins books (m1) say larger, better-connected learning networks retain and innovate more, and silos cause skill loss; that claim is about **connectivity for information and skill retention**, and it is itself contested at the archaeological scale (the population-size effect is reframed as learning-network connectivity, lab-demonstrated). Skyrms (m6) says correlation, meaning non-random structure that makes like meet like, is what rescues cooperation; Ostrom (m8) says small, dense, bounded groups are where the design principles hold; and this module's theorem says costly behaviours do not jump single weak ties. Those claims are about **closure for enforcement and complex contagion**. The two variables are different, and a design that maximises one degrades the other. The right mix is [H] for any group; that there is a trade-off is [E].

So the brief has to answer two questions separately. Where does the group need *information* to flow (across teams, from outside the org, from users), and are the bridges that carry it alive and held by people who will stay? Where does the group need *enforcement* (the mixed-motive behaviours from m7 that need normative expectations kept live), and is there enough closure there for monitoring to be a by-product and sanctions to be cheap? A norm that lives in a closed sub-team is protected by its density (the theorem's second direction) and invisible to the rest of the org; a norm announced across a sparse org has bridges but no closure and decays because nobody can see who is complying.

One more piece of structure worth holding, from the chapter on positive and negative relationships. **Structural balance** in signed graphs: triangles with three positive edges, or exactly one positive edge, are stable; the others (two friends who share an enemy is fine; two enemies who share a friend is strained) are not. Harary's theorem says a fully balanced network splits into at most two mutually hostile camps. Balance pressure predicts a two-faction split unless cross-cutting positive ties are maintained; when a group starts talking about "us" and "them", the structural remedy is deliberate positive ties that cut across the emerging boundary, which is what m2's structured-contact conditions look like on a graph.

And a warning about power that the bridges idea implies. Bargaining power in exchange networks depends on **outside options, not degree**: a node whose partners have no alternatives is powerful, while a central node in a long chain can be weak. If one person holds all the group's bridges, they are not just a single point of failure for information (m1's Tasmania risk in miniature) but the only route, and only-routes capture surplus. To flatten power in a team, give people alternatives: parallel ties, which is the same prescription complex contagion gave for a different reason.

ideas.title: Homophily has two sources; assume selection until longitudinal data show influence
ideas.body:
**Homophily** is the pervasive regularity that ties form disproportionately between similar people; Moody's school-friendship maps, where race predicts community structure, are the book's example, and McPherson, Smith-Lovin and Cook's review documents it across traits and settings. It matters for the course for two reasons. Homophily turns a network into clusters, and clusters (the first idea) block cascades of new behaviour. And homophily invites the most common causal mistake in reasoning about groups.

**Measuring it.** If a fraction p of nodes have a trait and q = 1 − p do not, random mixing would put 2pq of the edges across the boundary. The book's tiny example: 40 percent women, 60 percent men, so 0.48 of edges should be mixed-gender; if only 0.20 are, the network is strongly homophilous. The **2pq test** is a quick measure of how siloed a group is along any trait you care about (seniority, function, tenure, location), and it goes in the brief as a number you can actually compute from a contact graph or a survey of who talks to whom.

**Two mechanisms, hard to separate.** *Selection*: people choose similar friends. *Social influence*: friends make each other similar. Both produce identical cross-sectional patterns, and only longitudinal data can distinguish them. The book flags this for Christakis and Fowler's claim that obesity spreads through friendship networks; Shalizi and Thomas later showed that latent homophily (similarity on an unmeasured trait that drives both tie formation and the outcome) produces exactly the same patterns, so influence versus selection there remains unresolved. Crandall and colleagues' Wikipedia-editor study is the design that *can* separate them: similarity between editors rises sharply *before* their first interaction (selection) and keeps rising after it (influence); both are real. Ledger rule 35 makes the default explicit: **assume selection until shown otherwise.**

The organisational version is the inference "the people who thrive here are strikingly similar, so this community shapes people into that type". The weak-inference reading: similarity may be who was recruited, who self-selected in and who stayed, rather than anything membership did. The design consequence is not that influence is absent but that the levers differ: selection is fixed at the recruiting boundary (who is admitted, who is retained), influence by changing who talks to whom. A brief that proposes "culture change" without saying which of the two it is targeting has not diagnosed anything. And the humility consequence is that most claims about a group's "culture shaping people" are [H] unless someone has before-and-after data on the same people.

**Foci.** Feld's idea that people are tied to activities and groups gives three closures running in parallel: *triadic* (a friend of a friend), *focal* (two people sharing an activity) and *membership* (joining a friend's activity). Kossinets and Watts found that the chance of a new tie rises with each shared friend, with diminishing returns. This is the cheapest lever for building the parallel ties the second idea asked for: create shared foci (a rotation, a joint review, a cross-team on-call pairing) and closure does the rest. It is also the structural reading of m2's contact conditions: equal-status contact around a shared goal is a focus, and proximity alone is not.

A last caution against inferring mechanism from shape. Popularity in most systems is heavy-tailed, and a simple copying model (newcomers copy a random earlier node's choice with some probability, preferential attachment) produces heavy tails. But preferential attachment is one generator among many (ledger C53): a heavy tail does not establish copying, and extreme inequality of attention is the default outcome of copying rather than evidence of extreme quality differences. Early luck is amplified. Salganik, Dodds and Watts's artificial music markets are the demonstration: the same songs ranked very differently across eight worlds once download counts were visible.

ideas.title: Three kinds of copying with three fixes, and why short paths are never the bottleneck
ideas.body:
The book contains three models of people copying each other, and the ledger (rule 19) requires you to name which one you mean every time, because the fixes differ.

**Informational cascade (chapter 16).** People act in sequence and see what others *did* but not what they *knew*. Once two or three early movers agree, it is rational for everyone after to ignore their own signal and copy. The urn model shows the logic exactly: with private signals that are right two thirds of the time, the third person who sees two "blue" guesses and draws red should still guess blue, and from then on nobody's guess adds information; a wrong cascade happens about one time in five (illustrative computation). Cascades are wrong even when everyone reasons correctly, and they are *shallow*: choices after the cascade starts carry no new information, so a public signal or credible dissenter reverses them. Any sequential public decision (the senior person speaks first, a show of hands, a thread with visible early reactions) is an urn model. **Fix: collect private signals before anyone announces; randomise or reverse speaking order; make dissent cheap.** Bicchieri's pluralistic ignorance (m7) is a cascade over beliefs about norms, and this is the formal reason it collapses fast when the gap is published.

**Network effect (chapter 17).** Copying pays *because* others copy: the value of a tool, a format or a norm of showing up rises with the number of users. Aggregate adoption then has multiple equilibria, and the unstable one is a **tipping point**: below it adoption decays to zero, above it grows to a high stable level. Expectations are self-fulfilling. m4 met this model in population form (the Z-shaped curve). **Fix: cross the tipping point**, with a concentrated push in one subgroup rather than diffuse encouragement that leaks away, then stop.

**Coordination on a graph (chapter 19).** Copying pays because matching neighbours pays; the first idea's threshold and cluster theorem. **Fix: lower q, or seed inside the resisting clusters, or build wide bridges.**

Confusing them is the book's first listed misreading. Treating a show-of-hands vote as a tipping problem, or a documentation norm as an information problem, applies the wrong fix. The worked example asks you to say which of the three is producing the convergence you observe before proposing anything.

**Small worlds.** Two facts about large networks are surprising, and only one is usually understood. Short paths exist despite heavy clustering: Watts and Strogatz showed that a clustered lattice plus a few random long-range links has logarithmic average distance while keeping its clustering; homophily gives the lattice, weak ties give the shortcuts. But ordinary people can also *find* those paths with only local knowledge, and Watts-Strogatz cannot explain that. Kleinberg's theorem: with uniformly random shortcuts a greedy forwarder cannot home in; decentralised search is efficient only when the probability of a long-range link falls with distance to the power of the dimension of the space (one contact at every *scale* of distance, so each step can halve the remaining distance), and then greedy forwarding takes about (log n)² steps. Liben-Nowell and colleagues checked it on LiveJournal with a rank-based version and found the exponent close to ideal; Adamic and Adar found the analogue in an org chart.

The design consequence is that the coordination bottleneck in any group larger than a village is never distance; it is awareness (simple contagion) and thresholds (complex contagion). **Findability** is a separate, designable property: a group is navigable when each member has contacts at every scale (team, department, org, industry), a homophilous lattice with one cross-cutting tie per scale rather than random ones. Ask, in the brief, whether a person on one side of the org could route a question to the right person on the other side in a few hops; if not, the missing ties are at a specific scale, and that is where to add them.

worked_example.title: A distributed organisation wants to reduce silos (rubric only: you reason it through)
steps: Which face of connectedness is the problem: structure (few cross-ties between sub-teams) or behaviour (cross-ties exist but people do not act on what crosses them)? Draw the two separately. A structural fix for a behavioural problem adds ties nobody uses; a behavioural fix for a structural problem exhorts people who cannot see each other.

Is the goal information flow or norm adoption? Information is a simple contagion: a few weak bridges suffice, and the intervention is to find the people holding them and protect them. Norm adoption is a complex contagion: single liaisons cannot carry it; you need wide bridges (several parallel ties between sub-teams), moved sub-teams, or seeds inside each cluster.

Homophily check. For the trait that matters (function, seniority, site), compute or estimate whether cross-boundary edges fall below 2pq. Then say whether the similarity is selection (fixed at recruiting: who joined and stayed) or influence (membership changed people), and default to selection unless you have before-and-after data on the same people.

Navigability. Does each person have a contact at every scale (team, department, org)? If a question from one side cannot be routed to the right person on the other side in a few hops, name the scale where ties are missing and add cross-cutting ties there, not random ones.

Which of the three copying kinds is producing the convergence you observe? Sequential public decisions (informational cascade: collect private signals first, reverse speaking order); a tool or practice whose value rises with users (network effect: cross the tipping point in one subgroup); a norm that pays when neighbours match (coordination on a graph: lower q or seed inside clusters). Name it, then name the matching fix.

Required tags. [E] for the theorems (threshold, cluster density, 2pq, navigability exponent) and the structural weak-tie claim. [H] for the group's q, its cluster densities and any influence claim. [V] for how much closure (enforcement, trust) the org is willing to give up for bridging (information).

hinge.q: Twelve engineers vote by show of hands; the two most senior vote first, both yes; ten follow. Which kind of copying, and which fix?
options: Network effect; the vote is above its tipping point.
Coordination on a graph; lower the threshold.
Informational cascade; collect private judgments before anyone announces and reverse the speaking order.
Conformity as weakness; tell people to be independent.
diagnoses: Confuses the three kinds of copying (ledger rule 19). There is no payoff externality in a vote: nobody's outcome improves because more people voted yes; the copying here is informational.
Applies the chapter 19 fix to an informational problem. Thresholds and clusters concern behaviour that pays when neighbours match; a vote is a sequence of public signals.

Correct. After two visible agreeing signals, each later voter's rational move is to copy regardless of private judgment, so the ten votes may carry no information (`10` ch 16). Private simultaneous votes and juniors speaking first restore the signals.
Rational herding read as irrationality. The third person's copy is correct Bayesian play given what she can see; exhortation to independence does not change what she can see, the procedure does.

hinge.q: A norm has been adopted by a dense sub-team of ten. Management worries the sub-team's insularity will "hold the norm back" and proposes breaking it up across the org. Is that right?
options: Right: clusters slow spread.
Right, provided the members are influential.
Wrong: norms spread by information, so a newsletter is enough.
Wrong: the cluster's density protects the adopted norm; breaking it up returns each member to a neighbourhood below threshold. Keep the cluster and build wide bridges from it.
diagnoses: "Clusters are bad" (ledger X7, `10` misreadings). The density that would stop a norm entering from outside is the density that protects one adopted inside; the theorem runs both ways.

Influencer model of spread (ledger C30). Under threshold dynamics a scattered influential member is one neighbour among many for each node they reach; what matters is the fraction of each node's neighbours converted, not the prestige of any one.
Weak ties carry behaviour because they carry information (ledger C54). A newsletter is simple contagion: awareness crosses one tie, adoption of a costly practice needs several adopting neighbours.

Correct. Dispersed, each former member has mostly non-adopting neighbours and reverts; kept together, the cluster is a stable seed set, and parallel ties from it to each neighbouring sub-team are what a complex contagion needs (`10` ch 19; `07` ch 3).

hinge.q: The people who thrive in a community are strikingly similar. A member concludes the community "shapes people into that type". What is the correct default?
options: Accept it; influence is visible.
Assume selection (who joined and stayed) until longitudinal data show similarity rising after joining.
Reject it; communities cannot influence people.
Accept it if the community is large.
diagnoses: Influence assumed over selection (ledger C52). Cross-sectional similarity is produced identically by choosing similar members and by members changing each other; latent homophily mimics influence exactly.

Correct (`10` ch 4; ledger rule 35). Only before-and-after data on the same people, as in Crandall et al.'s Wikipedia design, separates the two; absent that, selection is the parsimonious default and the levers are at the recruiting boundary.
Over-correction. Both mechanisms are real where they have been measured; the rule is a default, not a denial.
Size as evidence of mechanism. Community size says nothing about whether similarity arose before or after joining.

hinge.q: Which is the robust version of the weak-ties claim?
options: Most useful information and most jobs come through weak ties.
Weak ties are more valuable than strong ties.
Weak ties tend to be the local bridges between clusters, so novelty enters through them; they are fragile and worth protecting.
Everyone is six steps from everyone, via weak ties.
diagnoses: The job-search claim as robust (ledger C51). Granovetter's finding was small-sample and retrospective; later large-scale work found most jobs via strong or moderately weak ties. Quote the structural claim only.
"Weak ties beat strong ties" (`10` misreadings). Closure supplies trust and enforcement; bridges supply information; neither is more valuable in general and cooperation needs both.

Correct. Every local bridge is a weak tie by Strong Triadic Closure, and Onnela et al. 2007 confirmed on a national phone graph that removing weak ties first shatters the network (`10` ch 3; ledger rule 33).
Six degrees as fact (ledger C50). The number is a median over the minority of completed chains; say "short paths exist" and leave the number out.

modules.brief_prompt: Add section s10, the network map and seeding plan. Sketch the group's clusters and bridges: who holds each bridge, and how many parallel ties exist between each pair of sub-groups. Record the homophily estimate (the 2pq comparison) for the trait that matters and whether you are assuming selection or influence. For the target norm, estimate q from the payoffs as members see them, name the cluster(s) that will block it, and place the seed set inside them. Say which of the three copying kinds is currently producing the group's convergence and the matching fix. Tag each: [E] for the theorems and the structural weak-tie claim, [H] for your q, densities and any influence claim. Prediction: which sub-group adopts first, and which never adopts through the current bridges.

modules.title: The four accounts reconciled and Gintis assessed
modules.hook: A traffic light tells each driver something different and nobody would gain by disobeying, given the others obey. A rule book tells everyone the same thing and is ignored. What does the light have that the book lacks, and what is your group's light?

attempt.prompt: Two product squads look at identical weekly metrics and reach opposite conclusions every week. Separately, a release cadence is half-assumed weekly and half-assumed fortnightly, and merges keep colliding. Diagnose each in one paragraph and say what you would change. Resist the first fix that comes to mind for each. No reading first.

objectives: State the four layers of 'how a group settles on a way of behaving' (Nash/ESS as stability test; Skyrms and Camerer for which stable state is reached absent intervention; Gintis for the public signal that aligns conjectures; Bicchieri for what must be true inside agents and how to measure it) and refuse to present any one as the theory.

Run Gintis's two-part norm test (epistemic: can everyone say what the norm requires of them and of others; motivational: does anyone gain by deviating given others comply, and is there a cheap sanction) and write a BPC line (beliefs, preferences, constraints) for a real group.
Assess each of Gintis's eight claims against the rest of the reading list, carrying out the two that hold and declining the unification.
Explain why persistent disagreement on shared data indicates different priors, and why the remedy is cultural alignment rather than more data.

ideas.title: Nash equilibrium is a social achievement, not a rational deduction
ideas.body:
Gintis's most durable contribution is a negative result with a constructive consequence. Rational choice, read modestly, is a theory of *consistent* preferences (the BPC model: beliefs, preferences, constraints), not of selfishness or cognitive perfection. Game theory is the indispensable grammar of interaction. But **game theory plus rationality cannot by itself predict what people do**, because Nash equilibrium cannot be justified from rationality alone.

The argument runs through epistemic game theory. Rationality plus **common knowledge of rationality** (everyone is rational, everyone knows it, everyone knows everyone knows, and so on) licenses only **rationalizability**: the strategies that survive iterated deletion of never-best-responses (Bernheim, Pearce). In most coordination games, in Chicken and in matching pennies, that leaves almost everything on the table. In a two-by-two coordination game every strategy is rationalizable. Nash requires additionally that players' *conjectures about each other* coincide, and nothing in individual rationality delivers that. The theorem is Aumann and Brandenburger (1995): for two players, mutual knowledge of rationality plus mutual knowledge of conjectures yields Nash; for more players, add a common prior and common knowledge of conjectures. These are *epistemic* conditions on what players know about each other, and no theory of individual reasoning produces them. So Nash is not "what rational agents do" but "what agents do once a social process has aligned their conjectures".

The rest of the reading list supports the corollary at every level. Camerer's coordination experiments (m5) show slow, path-dependent convergence rather than deduction; first-contact play is norm- and fairness-driven with one to two steps of reasoning. Schelling's focal points (m4) and Skyrms's dynamics (m6) do the selecting. The 1980s **refinement program** (perfect, proper, sequential, stable equilibria) tried to fix multiplicity with rationality-flavoured conditions and, in Gintis's reading, failed on its own terms: the refinements conflict, depend on arbitrary tremble structures, and lack an epistemic justification. Multiplicity is real, and its resolution is *social*, not logical. No book on the list dissents. Backward induction fares no better in sequential games: it requires common knowledge of rationality to hold even after moves that common knowledge says would never happen, and in the centipede game subjects go several rounds where the theory says take the pot at once.

The design consequence is a license the course uses everywhere: **stop trying to reason a group into equilibrium.** Meetings that derive the "obviously rational" plan reproduce the refinement program's failure; if you want a group to land on an equilibrium, something outside the players' rationality has to point at it. Pick a focal option, announce it, make it the default, and name the signal (the next idea). Ledger rule 14 states the same thing from the m3 side: Nash is a stability test, not a prediction and not an endorsement; with multiple equilibria it predicts nothing.

A note on what Gintis is *not* saying, since the misreading is common: he does not reject rational choice or game theory, and he does not show that people are irrational. He rejects selfishness as an add-on and the claim that rationality yields Nash; he keeps consistent-preference rationality as the core and wants game theory embedded in a theory of norms, not discarded. "Rational" is never contrasted with "fair" in this course (ledger rule 16), and the falsifiability worry about a model in which anything can be a preference is real and comes back in the fourth idea.

ideas.title: A norm is a choreographer: a public signal that makes an equilibrium focal and self-enforcing
ideas.body:
If aligned conjectures come from outside the players' heads, what supplies them? Gintis's answer is Aumann's **correlated equilibrium**, presented as a first-class concept rather than a footnote. A public signal draws a joint recommendation from a distribution over strategy profiles and privately tells each player their part. If, given the recommendation and what it implies about others' recommendations, no player wants to deviate, the distribution is a correlated equilibrium. Every Nash equilibrium is one; many correlated equilibria are not Nash. And Aumann's 1987 result closes the loop with the previous idea: Bayesian rationality plus a common prior yields exactly correlated (not Nash) equilibrium. The common prior is the choreographer in disguise.

The worked example is Chicken. Two pure Nash equilibria (one swerves, the other does not) and a mixed one with a poor expected payoff. A traffic light saying "go" or "wait" with equal probability gives each driver the good outcome half the time, better on average than the mixed equilibrium, and self-enforcing, because when it says "wait" you believe the other was told "go". That is the template for every norm in the book. **A social norm is a choreographer**: an external signal telling each player what to do and what others will do, such that following it is a best response when others follow it.

Chapter 10 says a working choreographer has two components, and the course turns them into a test. (1) **Epistemic**: the norm supplies the common conjecture; each person knows what others will do because the norm says so. Can every member state what the norm requires of *them* and of *others*? (2) **Motivational**: given that others comply, does anyone gain by deviating, and if so, is there a cheap sanction or a disposition that makes compliance a best response anyway? Most failed norms fail one of the two. A vague norm is a choreographer that does not choreograph; a clear norm nobody has reason to follow is a rule book. "First here has right of way", a traffic light, an office rota, a seating convention: one mechanism.

Chapter 11 applies it to property. The **bourgeois strategy** in Hawk-Dove (defend as incumbent, yield as intruder) is an evolutionarily stable, low-conflict convention and a correlated equilibrium with "who arrived first" as the signal. Uncorrelated play yields costly fights; conditioning on possession makes fights rare. For a group, ownership norms (who owns a codebase, a channel, a decision) reduce conflict primarily by being *clear and salient*, not by being fair; ambiguous ownership is a Hawk-Dove game without a correlating signal. Fairness matters for other reasons (legitimacy, willingness to sanction), which Ostrom and Bicchieri supply. The ledger's tags (rule 32, C57): the model is [E]; the claim that the endowment effect is the evolved psychology of property is [H]; and commons regimes are rule systems with monitoring, not possession cues alone.

Now the course's assessment, which is what the module is for. The choreographer model holds up *as a model*, and it is formally compatible with Bicchieri (a norm transforms a game via conditional preferences and expectations, and behaviour is an equilibrium of the transformed game conditioned on a shared cue) and with Skyrms's Lewis conventions. But it is **weaker than Bicchieri on diagnosis** (she separates empirical from normative expectations and tells you which to measure when a norm fails; Gintis treats compliance as a lump), **weaker than Ostrom on authorship** (her commons show choreographers written, monitored and revised by the players themselves, which the "external signal" framing obscures), and **weaker than Skyrms on origins** (he shows how correlation emerges without anyone designing it). Vanderschraaf's sympathetic review presses the point that the account still owes an explanation of *which* correlated equilibrium a society lands on and how the signal is learned: the Nash multiplicity gap, moved one level up. And the book runs no data horse race, so never write that correlated equilibrium "fits the data better than Nash" (ledger C58). What survives is one sharp design question that every Order-level book can now be read through: **what is the signal, and why does each person comply given the others do?**

ideas.title: Four layers, not four rivals: how a group settles on a way of behaving
ideas.body:
By this point the course has met four accounts of the same question, and a learner who has read them as competitors will write a brief that picks a favourite. The ledger (X5, rule 1) says they are layered, and the ordering is the course's own reconciliation.

**Layer 1: the stability test (Dixit et al., m3; Skyrms's ESS, m6).** Nash equilibrium asks whether any single member gains by deviating from a candidate pattern; an evolutionarily stable strategy asks whether a small group of mutants can invade it. This is a test applied to any proposed pattern of behaviour, a condition and not a verdict on goodness (mutual defection passes it). It says nothing about which of several stable patterns a group will reach.

**Layer 2: selection absent intervention (Skyrms and Camerer, m5 and m6).** Given the group's regime (how people are matched, how they update, how large the group is, whether they can talk), which stable pattern do the dynamics deliver? Under random mixing, best response, large groups and no communication: the risk-dominant one. Under correlation (small stable groups, success-visible imitation, public pledges, gradual growth, lower lone-cooperator cost): the payoff-dominant one becomes reachable. This layer has *no beliefs in it at all*; it is dynamics over behaviour, which is exactly its strength and its limit.

**Layer 3: the signal (Gintis, this module).** What a norm *does*: supply a public signal that aligns conjectures, so that the good pattern is focal and each person's compliance is a best response given the others'. Theorem-backed as a claim about equilibrium; silent on where the signal comes from and on what happens inside people when it fails.

**Layer 4: the expectations inside agents (Bicchieri, m7).** What must be true inside people for the signal to work: an empirical expectation that enough others comply and a normative expectation that enough others expect them to, possibly sanction-backed; and how to measure both, so that when a norm fails you can say which expectation is missing.

Ostrom (m8) and the network book (m9) sit across the layers rather than in one: Ostrom shows how participants build and repair the signal and the sanctions (layers 3 and 4, authored from inside), and Easley and Kleinberg decide whether the signal is *seen* across the whole network (a choreographer not visible across the network does not correlate play; a group with weak cross-ties can host two priors).

Why the order matters. Teaching Bicchieri before Skyrms would make the learner treat expectations as the whole story and miss that basin size decides outcomes even with no beliefs at all; teaching Gintis alone would give the signal without the psychology of its failure. Ledger rule 1's instruction is precise: never present one of the four as "the" theory of norms. The formal relations between the layers are [E]; **which layer bites in a given group is [H]**, and it is the single most useful hypothesis the brief can state. A contribution norm posted on a visible board that everyone can recite and nobody follows has passed layer 3's epistemic half and failed its motivational half; the repair comes from layer 4 (are the normative expectations live?) and from Ostrom (is there a cheap, graduated sanction?). A rollout that fails although the pledge was clear and the norm was measured has a layer-2 problem: the regime delivers risk dominance regardless. The worked example walks the learner's own v0 fix through all four in order.

This is also why the module declines the unification (the fourth idea). The layering *is* a map of how the books fit together. Chapter 12 of Gintis lists five compatible principles and asserts they suffice; compatibility is not unification, and the ordering of interventions comes from the other books and from your own diagnostic, not from the framework.

ideas.title: Strong reciprocity and BPC: what to carry, what to decline
ideas.body:
Two of Gintis's claims are contested in ways that matter for the brief, and the course's verdicts on them are fixed by the ledger.

**Strong reciprocity.** Chapter 3 marshals the experimental economics that shows people are not selfish: ultimatum rejections, public goods with costly punishment, trust games, and the cross-cultural games in fifteen small-scale societies that Gintis co-authored, where offer *levels* vary with market integration and everyday cooperation while pure self-interest is rejected everywhere. He reads the evidence as support for **strong reciprocity**: an evolved predisposition to cooperate conditionally and to punish defectors at personal cost, even in one-shot anonymous settings, and this supplies the motivational half of the choreographer.

The lab facts replicate well; rejection of pure self-interest is about as secure as anything in behavioural science. The *evolutionary* claim is disputed. Binmore and Shaked argue that one-shot lab behaviour is consistent with subjects mis-applying heuristics tuned for repeated interaction, and that learning erodes cooperation in many designs; Guala's field review argues that evidence for *costly* punishment in small-scale societies is thin, and that sanctioning in the wild is mostly cheap (gossip, ostracism, withdrawal). Both are background references, not verified this session, but a well-known dispute. And Ostrom's cases, the strongest field evidence on the list, show graduated, low-cost, participant-run sanctioning rather than heroic costly punishment. The ledger splits the claim (X4, rule 4): **willingness to pay to punish unfair intentions in the lab is [E]; "strong reciprocity is an evolved trait" is [H]; real-world sanctioning is mostly cheap and graduated, so design on the cheap version.** The design lesson survives the dispute: members will sanction free riders at some cost to themselves, so give them a low-cost, legitimate, proportionate channel, or punishment goes underground. Diagnostic item d3 is built from this correction, and the misreading to avoid is "the book proves that norms are internalised by evolution"; it argues it, and provides no evolutionary models of its own.

**BPC and the anomalies.** Chapter 1 reframes prospect-theory anomalies (loss aversion, reference dependence) and hyperbolic discounting as *state-dependent* preferences: if the current endowment is part of the state, a loss-averse agent can still be consistent. The move is productive as bookkeeping. But the ledger (X16) records the tension with the social-psychology material: construal, framing, motivated reasoning and naive realism are shifts in *beliefs* with presentation and mood, not tidily captured as state-dependent preferences; Camerer's learning chapter shows adaptive, path-dependent behaviour rather than fixed-point rationality; and Henrich shows preferences are culturally acquired and vary across societies, which BPC accommodates as data but does not predict. The verdict is Gintis's own on claim 3: partially holds up, overstated. Once anything can be a preference the model constrains little without auxiliary theory, which is what the rest of the reading list is; Gintis's reply that revealed-preference axioms such as transitivity are testable is correct but weaker than the rhetoric.

What to carry into the brief, then, is the **BPC line as a discipline**: before proposing an intervention, write down what members believe about each other, what they value (including status and fairness, not just money), and what constrains them. Most "incentive" fixes change constraints while beliefs about what others will do stay the same, which is why they fail. Do not carry the claim that BPC *explains* construal effects, and note the falsifiability worry in the tag. Prefer the norm to the incentive when both are available (the disposition already exists and is cheaper to maintain; large explicit incentives can crowd it out), tagged [H] because crowding-out is real but context-dependent; this is tension t12 in m11.

ideas.title: Common priors are culture: align beliefs by shared frames, not more dashboards
ideas.body:
Savage's axioms make a rational agent Bayesian, but they say nothing about where the prior comes from. The **common-prior assumption** (the Harsanyi doctrine: all players' beliefs derive from one prior updated on private information) is not derivable from rationality; it is a substantive claim that agents share a *culture*. Aumann's agreeing-to-disagree theorem shows how much work the assumption does: Bayesians with a common prior whose posteriors are common knowledge cannot disagree. Gintis's move is to replace "common prior" with "shared cultural frame", which is empirically checkable, and to locate the source of shared priors in cultural transmission, imitation and language: his most direct link to the Origins level.

This is the one place where the synthesis is well supported by the rest of the list, and the course's verdict on claim 4 is that it holds up. Conformist and prestige-biased learning (m1) are exactly how priors converge within groups and diverge between them; the cross-cultural game results show that "priors" about fair offers are socially shared and vary with the economics of daily life. Easley and Kleinberg (m9) add the qualifier: convergence follows network structure, so a group with weak cross-ties can host two priors, and the 2pq test tells you where the boundary is.

The diagnostic reading is the one the cold attempt targets. When two sub-teams keep reaching different conclusions from the same data, week after week, the first instinct is an information intervention: more metrics, a better dashboard, a shared report. If the disagreement persists on *shared* data, that instinct is wrong; the problem is different priors, that is, different cultures. The intervention is cultural: shared definitions of the metrics, joint training, shared stories about what past numbers meant, a common vocabulary. Aligning beliefs is a cultural intervention, not an information intervention, and it is tagged [E] for the direction (supported by Henrich and Laland) and [H] for the specific alignment intervention in your group.

The same chapter reframes mixed strategies. At a mixed Nash equilibrium each player is indifferent among the mixed strategies, so nothing motivates mixing in exactly the equilibrium proportions. Gintis prefers reading a mixed equilibrium as a *conjecture about the opponent population*, sustained by social process: a fraction who monitor and a fraction who do not is a **population fact** stabilised by norms and learning, not a randomisation each person performs. That is Skyrms's replicator picture (m6) and Camerer's type distribution (m5) stated in epistemic terms, and it means a group's "mix" of behaviours is something to measure and shift, not a coin each member flips.

Finally, the assessment the module is built around: what to carry out of *The Bounds of Reason*. Two things. (1) The epistemic critique of Nash and the choreographer idea, which sharpen every Order-level book into one design question: *what is the signal, and why does each person comply given the others do?* (2) The discipline of writing down beliefs, preferences and constraints before proposing an intervention. Do not carry out the claim that the behavioural sciences have been unified, or that norm-following is settled evolutionary fact. Reviewers (Tyran, Rouchier, Field, Vanderschraaf; existence verified) praise the exposition of epistemic game theory and call the unification programmatic: chapter 12 lists five compatible principles (gene-culture coevolution, the sociopsychological theory of norms, game theory, the rational actor model, complexity theory) and asserts they suffice, but derives no result that sociology or anthropology lacked, and the complexity principle is not used at all. Rouchier's generous reading is the right one: game theory as a *complement* that keeps social theory honest about incentives and expectations, and social theory as the supplier of the priors, preferences and signals game theory needs. On that reading the book is right and modest, and "unification" is a title. Two things not to do, per ledger rule 31: never write "the unification", and never attribute a review to Binmore; none was found, and Binmore and Gintis in fact agree on the epistemic critique and fight over strong reciprocity and group selection.

worked_example.title: Your own v0 fix, re-run through the four layers (rubric only)
steps: Stability. Is the pattern your v0 fix proposes an equilibrium at all? Ask the m3 question of the fixed state: would any single member gain by deviating alone, once everyone else is doing it? If yes, the fix is not a resting point and will need continuous enforcement; say so, and decide whether that is what you want.

Selection. Absent the fix, which stable state does the group's regime deliver? Name the regime: how members are matched (random or stable subgroups), how they update (success-copying or majority-copying), how large the group is, whether they can talk. Then say whether your fix changes the *regime* or only the *payoffs*. A fix that only sweetens the joint payoff leaves a risk-dominant regime risk-dominant.

Signal. What public cue tells each member which equilibrium is in play (a rota, a pinned cadence, a dashboard, a template, a ritual)? Run the two-part test: can everyone state what the norm requires of them and of others; does anyone gain by deviating given others comply, and is there a cheap sanction? Then check with m9 whether the signal is visible across the whole network or only inside one cluster.

Expectations. Which empirical and normative expectations must be live for the signal to work, and how will they be measured (the m7 two-step items)? If the normative expectation is absent, the choreographer's motivational half has failed and no amount of signal clarity repairs it.

Write the BPC line for the group: what members believe about each other, what they value (including status and fairness), what constrains them. Then say which layer the v0 fix addressed and which it ignored.

Required tags. [E] for the formal relations between the layers. [H] for which layer bites in this group. [V] for any claim about which equilibrium ought to be chosen; the layers tell you what is stable and reachable, not what is good.

hinge.q: A contribution norm is posted on a visible board; everyone can state it; compliance is still low. Which half has failed, and which reading repairs it?
options: The epistemic half; make the board more visible.
The motivational half: some members gain by deviating and no sanction bites; repair with Ostrom's graduated sanctions and Bicchieri's normative expectations.
Neither; people are irrational.
The evolved norm psychology is absent in this group.
diagnoses: All norm failures as information failures. The epistemic test is passed (everyone can state the norm); more visibility adds nothing to a signal already seen.

Correct. A choreographer needs both halves; here compliance is not a best response given others' compliance, so the repair is a cheap graduated sanction (m8) and live normative expectations (m7), plus Camerer's warning that cooperation decays without feedback (`11` ch 10).

"Gintis shows people are irrational" (`11` misreadings). He defends consistent-preference rationality; low compliance with a clear norm nobody has reason to follow is exactly what consistent preferences produce.

Strong reciprocity as a settled trait that should have carried compliance (ledger rule 4). The evolved-trait claim is [H]; the design lesson is to supply a cheap sanctioning channel, not to expect an innate disposition to do the work.

hinge.q: Which statement about the four accounts is the course's position?
options: Bicchieri's is the correct theory of norms; the others are approximations.
Gintis unified them.
They are layered: stability test, selection absent intervention, the aligning signal, the expectations inside agents; which layer bites in a group is a hypothesis.
Skyrms's dynamics make the others redundant.
diagnoses: One account as "the" theory (ledger rule 1). Bicchieri is the best of the four on diagnosis and measurement, and says nothing about basin size or where the signal comes from.
"The unification" (ledger C55). Chapter 12 shows compatibility and derives no new result; the ordering of interventions comes from the other books.
Correct (ledger X5). The formal relations are [E]; which layer is binding for a particular group is the [H] the brief must state and test.

Dynamics without beliefs as the whole story (ledger C41). Skyrms's agents have no expectations to measure and his results do not rescue true PDs; institutions and expectations are what the models recommend.

hinge.q: What is the durable contribution of *The Bounds of Reason* for the brief?
options: That correlated equilibrium fits data better than Nash.
That the behavioural sciences now share one theory.
That Binmore's review discredited the book.
The epistemic critique of Nash and the choreographer idea, which turn every Order-level book into one question: what is the signal, and why does each person comply given the others do?
diagnoses: An empirical superiority claim the book never tests (ledger C58). The argument for correlated equilibrium is conceptual (Aumann 1987); there is no data horse race.
Programmatic unification read as achieved (ledger rule 31). Reviewers call it a framework and a checklist; no discipline has to change a model because of chapter 12.

An attributed review that was not found (ledger C56). Binmore and Gintis agree on the epistemic critique and disagree about strong reciprocity and group selection; do not cite a review that does not exist.
Correct (`11` net assessment). Carry the critique, the choreographer's two-part test and the BPC discipline; decline the unification and the settled-evolutionary-fact reading of norm-following.

hinge.q: Ambiguous ownership of a shared codebase produces recurring fights. Which reading of Gintis's chapter 11 is right?
options: Assign the fairest owner and fights will fall most.
Ownership fights are innate territoriality; only a manager's dominance stops them.

Assign a clear owner, even somewhat arbitrarily, because an ambiguous ownership cue leaves a hawk-dove game without a correlating signal; fairness matters for legitimacy and sanctioning, which Ostrom and Bicchieri supply.
Ownership is a rule system, so write a rule.
diagnoses: Fairness as the mechanism. The bourgeois convention works by being salient and mutually recognised; a fair but ambiguous allocation can produce more fights than a clear arbitrary one.

The endowment effect as evolved property psychology treated as [E] (ledger C57), plus dominance over prestige (`01`). The cue-only story is a model; the psychology is [H]; and dominance is the wrong channel for a convention people must copy.
Correct (ledger rule 32). The signal ends the hawk-dove fight; legitimacy and willingness to sanction are separate goods that the fairness of the allocation and the process supply.
Partly right, wrong level. A rule nobody monitors is not a signal (`09` rules-in-use); the cue has to be visible and acted on to correlate play.

modules.brief_prompt: Add section s11, the signal and the BPC statement. For each of the group's central coordination problems, name the public signal that tells members which equilibrium is in play and say whether it is visible across the whole network or only inside one cluster. Record the two-part test result (epistemic, motivational) for the group's main norm. Write one BPC line: what members believe about each other, what they value including status and fairness, what constrains them. State which of the four layers the v0 fix addressed and which it ignored. Tag each: [E] for the formal relations, [H] for which layer bites, [V] for any claim about which equilibrium ought to hold. Prediction: which layer, if addressed alone, moves behaviour in this group, and which does nothing without the others.

modules.title: Integration: tensions, decision rules, the diagnostic path
modules.hook: Five experts diagnose the same failing community: one says its learning network is broken, one says the game is a PD, one says it is below critical mass, one says the norm lacks normative expectations, one says the seed sat outside the cluster. All five are right. In what order do you act?

attempt.prompt: Take the five disagreements below and, for each, write the condition under which each side is right. Do not pick a side; write an 'if the group is like X, do A; if like Y, do B' rule, and mark the condition as a hypothesis about your own group rather than a fact about groups in general. (i) Sweeten the joint payoff vs cut the lone-cooperator cost. (ii) Mix people more vs keep stable clusters. (iii) Explain vs model. (iv) Publish the descriptive norm vs never advertise prevalence. (v) Install institutions vs let structure do the work.

objectives: Walk the diagnostic path from a real failure to a ranked fix set, in order: arithmetic; situation and construal; game shape; curve shape and threshold; type mix and amendment; regime and correlation; norm classification and expectations; institutional checklist; network seeding; signal and layers.
State each of the thirteen tensions (t01-t13) as a conditional decision rule with the condition tagged [H], and say which tension a given disagreement in the brief falls under.
Re-tag Brief v0 line by line with a changelog, fill the open-hypotheses and value-commitments registers, and identify the single most important missing decision.

State the course's certainty gradient (theorems; lab mechanisms for direction; institutional and network prescriptions as hypotheses; the choice of equilibrium as a value) and refuse any [E] that is not a ledger [E].

ideas.title: Diagnose before prescribing: the ten-step path
ideas.body:
Most v0 briefs skip to a lever. The learner's first page usually said either that the people were the problem or that an incentive would fix it, and every module since has supplied a reason to distrust that shortcut. The integration module fixes an order of diagnosis. The *order* is the course's own choice and is tagged [V]; each step's content is [E] from the source named. The rule that binds the whole path: **no fix is proposed at any step before that step's diagnosis, and at least one step must conclude "not the binding constraint here".**

1. **Is it arithmetic?** (Schelling, m4.) Check accounting identities and constraints before motives: mentors to mentees, reviewers to reviews, seats to attendees. A failure that is a counting problem has no behavioural fix.
2. **Is it the situation?** (Gilovich et al., m2.) Write the situational alternative to the dispositional story: workload, ambiguity, visibility, ownership, deliberation design, construal. Strike through any lever from the failed-replication list.
3. **What is the game shape?** (Dixit et al., m3.) Draw the matrix with payoffs as members see them and ask whether a member gains by defecting when everyone else cooperates. PD, stag hunt, chicken, battle of the sexes or coordination; each has its own fix set.
4. **Is behaviour contingent, and where is the threshold?** (Schelling and the network book's population models, m4.) Draw the two curves. Multi-person PD (needs rules), coordination with a tipping point (needs seeding above critical mass), or stable interior mix (leave alone). Find the low-threshold members.
5. **Which amendment?** (Camerer, m5.) Is the departure from the formal prediction driven by social preferences and fairness frames, by limited iterated reasoning, or by learning and early-round lock-in? Describe the group as a distribution of types, not a representative agent.
6. **What regime, and what correlation?** (Skyrms, m6.) Near-random mixing with frequent re-evaluation, or stable subgroups with visible success? Which correlation device is cheapest, and what is the lone-cooperator cost?
7. **What kind of norm, and which expectations?** (Bicchieri, m7.) Descriptive, convention, social or moral; measure the two expectations; read the pluralistic-ignorance gap; check the cues.
8. **Which principles are missing, and at which rule level?** (Ostrom, m8.) Run the checklist with a scope flag; find the level (operational, collective-choice, constitutional) where the reform is stalling; design the sanctions ladder and the by-product monitoring.
9. **Where in the network?** (Easley and Kleinberg, m9.) Clusters, bridges, q, seed set; which of the three copying kinds is producing the convergence; selection before influence.
10. **What is the signal, and which layer bites?** (Gintis and the four layers, m10.) Name the public cue; run the two-part test; write the BPC line; say which of stability, selection, signal and expectations the fix addresses.

The hook's five experts are each standing on one step, and each is right about their step. The order of *action* depends on which step is the binding constraint for this group, and that is a hypothesis: you rank the fixes, attach one prediction per fix that could be checked in the group within three months, and state what would make you abandon the main one. The rubric for the worked example is the path itself: every step names its source; no fix precedes its diagnosis; at least one step is declared non-binding; nothing in the fix set appears on the failed-replication list; every [E] is a ledger [E].

Two things the path is not. It is not a claim that every group has every problem; the point of "not the binding constraint here" is to let most steps be short. And it is not in the sources; none of the eleven books proposes a diagnostic order across the others, which is why the order carries a [V] and why the capstone scores the *discipline* of diagnosis before fix more heavily than any particular fix.

ideas.title: The tensions are conditional rules, not contradictions
ideas.body:
Where two books on the list disagree, the ledger records both and states a conditional resolution. The integration module turns each into a decision rule of the form "if the group is like X, do A; if like Y, do B", and the whole point is that the *condition* is a hypothesis about your group, to be tested, never a fact about groups in general. Picking a side is the error the cold attempt is built to surface. The thirteen tensions, by id:

- **t01 Copying biases vs copying strategies; copying vs teaching** (Henrich vs Laland). Use Henrich's bias list as the levers (whom people copy) and Laland's tournament logic as the reason copying pays (demonstrators pre-filter). Spread *norm adherence* by models, prestige and expectations; transfer a *skill with hidden structure* by explicit teaching. Never collapse into "explanation does not work" or "just document it".
- **t02 Strong reciprocity as evolved trait vs cheap graduated sanctioning.** Lab willingness to punish is [E]; the evolved trait is [H]; field sanctioning is mostly cheap. Design on the cheap version.
- **t03 Four accounts of how a group settles.** Layered, not rival: stability test, selection, signal, expectations. Which layer bites is [H].
- **t04 Risk vs payoff dominance; clusters block vs help.** Regime and learning rule decide. Risk dominance under random mixing, best response, large groups, no talk; payoff dominance reachable through correlation. Clusters help only under success-copying; a dense cluster blocks entry from outside and protects adoption inside.
- **t05 Stable social preferences vs cued norm compliance; internalised vs conditional.** Model fairness as a distribution of sensitivities conditional on cues; assume every norm conditional until it survives a collapse of expectations.
- **t06 Designed vs copied-and-evolved institutions.** Copy a visibly successful peer's norm package, then craft incrementally with those bound by the rules. Neither "design from scratch" nor "just copy" is [E].
- **t07 PD vs stag hunt; does cheap talk work.** Classify first by the defection question. Talk is [E] in the lab and in stag-hunt models; expect it to decay without sanctions or repetition where defection dominates.
- **t08 Cultural group selection and culture-drove-brains.** [H], never load-bearing; within-group mechanisms are the [E] part.
- **t09 Connectivity vs closure.** Connectivity for information and skill retention; closure for enforcement and complex contagion. The right mix is [H].
- **t10 Descriptive-norm messaging.** Always pair descriptive with injunctive; never advertise prevalence of misbehaviour.
- **t11 Anomalies as preferences vs unstable beliefs.** BPC as bookkeeping only; do not claim it explains construal effects.
- **t12 Incentives vs norms** (crowd-out; Gilovich ch 7, Dixit ch 14, Gintis). Prefer the norm where the disposition exists; expect a large explicit incentive to displace it. Crowd-out is real but context-dependent, so the condition is [H].
- **t13 Change expectations vs change structure** (Bicchieri vs Easley-Kleinberg and Skyrms). Expectations where the group is one reference network and the signal is seen by all; structure where clusters and bridges decide who sees the signal.

Here are the five attempt disagreements resolved as the module expects. (i) Cut the lone-cooperator cost, because it moves the watershed more; sweeten the joint payoff only when the lone-cooperator cost is already low (t04). (ii) Keep stable clusters while a norm is young *if members copy success*; if they copy the majority, clusters will not spread it and you need success-visibility first; mix for information flow, never for norm spread (t04, t09). (iii) Model for adherence, teach for hidden structure (t01). (iv) Publish only when paired with an injunctive signal and only the compliant share; never the prevalence of misbehaviour (t10). (v) Let structure do the work in a stag hunt with success-copying and stable subgroups; install institutions (monitoring, graduated sanctions, standing) where the defection question says PD or where the group is too large for by-product monitoring (t06, t07).

A correctly stated rule has a condition, names the source, and tags the condition [H]. "Always keep stable clusters" is a side. "Clusters help because one online experiment showed it" is a background study promoted to a theorem with the condition missing. The open-hypotheses register (s12) is where each rule's condition goes, with the test and the date.

ideas.title: Certainty drops as you climb: the tag discipline and the changelog
ideas.body:
The unified model reads like a building, and certainty falls as you go up. At the foundation, the Origins mechanisms (copying biases, norm psychology) are [E] and their weights in any group are [H]; the deep-time story (cultural group selection, culture-drove-brains) is [H]. In the Mechanisms band, the formal results are theorems and the replicated lab mechanisms are [E], but any group's classification is [H]. In the Order band, the models and the systematic reviews are [E]; every prescription for a particular group is [H]; and the choice of which equilibrium ought to hold is [V]. At the roof, the four layers are a map, and which layer bites is [H]. This is ledger rules 27 and 40 in one sentence: **use lab results for mechanisms and directions, never as field point estimates, and quote no number that is not in the ledger's section 4.**

The most common capstone error, and the one the scoring penalises most, is tagging a lab mechanism as [E] *for the learner's own group*. "Communication roughly doubles cooperation" is [E] as a lab direction; "our retro will double contributions" is [H]. "The stag hunt is formally distinct from the PD" is [E]; "our team is a stag hunt" is [H] until the defection question has been answered with the group's own payoffs, and remains a hypothesis even then, because self-reported payoffs are construal (m2). The second most common error is the reverse: tagging a value as a hypothesis. "Member governance is worth the slower decisions" is not testable; it is [V], and pretending it is [H] hides the commitment from the reader who most needs to see it.

The changelog is how the discipline becomes visible. Brief v0 was tagged on day one, badly, and the instruction then was to do it anyway. Now re-tag v0 line by line against the current version and record, for every tag that changed, why: which module, which ledger rule, which measurement. A typical changelog moves several dispositional [E]s ("two people are coasting") to situational [H]s after m2; converts an incentive fix tagged [E] into a [V] about what the group should reward after m3 and t12; moves "clusters slow spread" from [E] to its opposite after m9; and, almost always, adds a line that was missing entirely: who has standing to change the rules, and what the public signal is.
