Those two are the decisions learners skip most (per the worked examples in m8 and m10), and the third hinge question asks about them for that reason.

Three registers close the brief. **s12, open hypotheses**: every [H] in the brief, each with the test that would settle it and the date by which the learner will have run it; this is where the tension conditions live. **s13, value commitments**: every [V], stated plainly so that a reader can disagree with the values without disputing the evidence. **s14, measurement plan and ninety-day predictions**: three predictions with dates, the first cheap change that produces information and standing, and what would make the learner abandon the main hypothesis. The capstone's critique prompt will attack tagging discipline first, contradictions with the course second, internal inconsistency third, and the single most important missing decision last; the changelog is the learner's evidence on the first count.

A note on the sources' own limits, because the capstone rewards knowing them. The ledger's section 6 lists what the eleven books cannot settle: whether cultural group selection is an engine or a redescription; whether norm-following is internalised or conditional-but-looks-internalised; whether one-shot punishment is an evolved trait; whether payoff dominance is stable under noisy best response or only reachable transiently; whether Ostrom's principles transfer to digital commons; whether influence can be separated from selection without longitudinal data; whether descriptive and normative expectations can be disentangled in the field. Where the brief touches one of these, the honest tag is [H] with a note that the sources are open, and the honest prediction is one the learner's own group can check. That is the whole method: the reading list gives mechanisms and directions; the group gives the numbers.

worked_example.title: Your group through the ten-step path in one page (rubric only)
steps: Walk the ten steps in order for your own group, one short paragraph each: arithmetic; situation; game shape; curve shape and threshold; amendment; regime and correlation; norm kind and expectations; missing principles and rule level; network position and seeding; signal and layer. Each paragraph names its source module and book.

At each step, write the diagnosis before any fix, and be willing to write 'not the binding constraint here' with a one-line reason. A page in which every step finds a problem has not diagnosed anything; at least one step must be declared non-binding.

For every disagreement you meet between steps (mix or cluster; explain or model; incentive or norm; expectations or structure), name the tension by id (t01-t13) and write its rule with the condition tagged [H] and entered in the open-hypotheses register.

Rank the fixes. Each fix carries: the step it came from, one prediction checkable in the group within ninety days with a date, and a tag per claim. Check the fix set against the failed-replication list (ego depletion, priming, power posing, watching eyes, the Stanford Prison Experiment, groupthink as a syndrome, IAT training) and remove anything that appears on it.

Audit the tags: every [E] must be a ledger [E]; every claim about this particular group is [H]; every claim about which equilibrium ought to hold, or what the group should reward, is [V]. Then write the changelog against Brief v0 and name the single most important decision v0 was missing.

Rubric: every step names its source; no fix precedes its diagnosis; at least one step concludes 'not binding'; nothing on the failed-replication list survives; every [E] is a ledger [E]; the missing-decision line is present. This page is Brief v5, the capstone's input.

hinge.q: A learner's brief tags "our team is a stag hunt" as [E]. Correct?
options: Yes; the stag hunt is a theorem.
No; it is [H] until the defection question has been answered with the group's own payoffs, and even then it remains a hypothesis.
No; it should be [V].
Yes, if the team says so.
diagnoses: Tags the formal distinction's status onto the group's classification (ledger rule 13: [E] for the distinction, [H] for the classification). The theorem is about the game; whether this team is playing it is an empirical question.
Correct. Classification depends on payoffs as members see them, which are construal-laden and measured indirectly; the tag stays [H] with a test in the open-hypotheses register (ledger rules 13, 27).
Confuses an empirical hypothesis with a value commitment. Whether the team is a stag hunt is a fact to be tested, not a preference about how it should be run.
Self-report of payoffs as evidence. Construal and naive realism (`03`) mean members' descriptions of their own incentives are data about beliefs, not a settled classification.

hinge.q: Which is a correctly stated tension rule?
options: "Always keep stable clusters."
"Mixing spreads information and norms alike."
"Keep stable clusters while a norm is young if members copy success; if they copy the majority, clusters will not spread it and you need success-visibility first."
"Clusters help because Centola proved it."
diagnoses: A side, not a condition. A tension rule has an 'if' whose condition is tagged [H]; an unconditional instruction is what the cold attempt is designed to catch.
Simple and complex contagion collapsed (ledger rule 34). Information crosses one weak tie; costly behaviour needs several adopting neighbours, so mixing helps one and hurts the other (t09).
Correct (t04; ledger X7). The condition is the group's learning rule, which is a hypothesis about the group and goes in the open-hypotheses register with a test.
One background study promoted to a theorem, with the condition missing. Centola 2010 is background; the theorem is the cluster-density result, and it comes with the learning-rule condition.

hinge.q: A brief's single most important missing decision is most often:
options: The incentive scheme.
Who has standing to change the rules, and what the public signal is.
The values statement.
The team-building event.
diagnoses: Incentives as the default lever. Most v0 briefs already have one; the capstone penalises fixes proposed before diagnosis, and t12 says a large explicit incentive can displace the norm it is meant to support.

Correct. The collective-choice level (`09` ch 2: nobody affected can legitimately change the rule) and the epistemic half of the norm (`11` ch 10: no cue tells members which equilibrium is in play) are the two decisions learners skip most, per the worked examples in m8 and m10.
Norms as values (ledger C43). A values statement targets the wrong object when the norm is conditional; it is neither standing nor signal.
Proximity as contact (`03` ch 10). Contact effects need equal-status, goal-directed, institutionally supported interaction; an event supplies proximity and none of the conditions.

modules.brief_prompt: Re-tag Brief v0 line by line against the current version and write a changelog: every tag that changed, and why (module, ledger rule or measurement). Fill s12, the open-hypotheses register, with every [H] in the brief, its test and the date; fill s13, the value-commitments register, with every [V] stated plainly; write s14, the measurement plan and ninety-day predictions (three predictions with dates; the first cheap change that produces information and standing; what would make you abandon the main hypothesis). Name the single most important decision v0 was missing. This is Brief v5, the capstone's input.
